definition: An ordinary process that the Linux kernel isolates with namespaces and limits with cgroups, running from an image's filesystem plus a private, disposable writable layer.
A read-only, layered filesystem snapshot plus metadata such as the default command and user. One image can be the template for any number of containers.
The two kernel features behind containers: namespaces control what a process can see (processes, network, mounts), and cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O).
The set of files sent to the builder by `docker build`, usually the directory you pass as the last argument, minus anything matched by `.dockerignore`. `COPY` can only read from it.
Writing `CMD` or `ENTRYPOINT` as a JSON array, such as `["node", "dist/server.js"]`, so the program runs as PID 1 without a shell and receives stop signals directly.
Stored results of earlier build steps. A step is reused when its instruction and inputs are unchanged; the first changed step and every step after it rebuild.
The polite stop signal Docker and Kubernetes send to PID 1 before a forced SIGKILL. Apps should handle it by finishing in-flight work and exiting cleanly.
A Dockerfile with several `FROM` stages where only the final stage ships, so compilers, dev dependencies and sources stay in earlier stages and out of the production image.
A file listing patterns to exclude from the build context, such as `node_modules`, `.git` and `.env` files, which speeds up builds and keeps secrets out of images.
A minimal base image containing only a language runtime and its libraries, with no shell or package manager, which shrinks the attack surface and the vulnerability report.
A SHA-256 hash that identifies an image's exact content. Unlike a tag, it can never point to different bytes, so pinning by digest guarantees every node runs the same image.
A BuildKit feature, `RUN --mount=type=secret`, that exposes a credential to one build step as a file or environment variable without writing it into any image layer.
One component of a Compose application, such as `api` or `db`, defined in `compose.yaml` and reachable from other services on the project network by its service name.
Docker-managed storage that exists independently of containers, used for data such as database files that must survive container removal. `docker compose down -v` deletes it.
A command Docker runs inside a container on a schedule to decide whether it is healthy. Compose can make other services wait for it with `condition: service_healthy`.
A development mode, started with `docker compose up --watch`, that syncs edited files into running containers or rebuilds the image when files such as the lockfile change.
The pattern behind Kubernetes controllers: continuously observe actual state, compare it with the desired state stored in the API, and act to close the difference.
The smallest unit Kubernetes schedules: one or more containers that share a network identity and volumes. Pods are disposable and replaced, not repaired.
A Kubernetes object that keeps a set of identical Pods running through ReplicaSets and replaces them gradually when the Pod template changes.
A query over key-value labels that Kubernetes objects use to find each other, for example a Service selecting the Pods it sends traffic to.
A stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of ready Pods chosen by a label selector. Types include ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer.
Objects that hold configuration for Pods, injected as environment variables or files. Secrets are for credentials but are only base64-encoded, so access control matters.
A Kubernetes scope for object names, permissions and quotas, typically one per app or team. It does not block network traffic without a NetworkPolicy.
A periodic check that decides whether a Pod should receive traffic. Failing removes the Pod from Service endpoints without restarting it, and it gates rolling updates.
A periodic check that decides whether a container is stuck. Failing restarts the container, so it must not depend on databases or other services.
Per-container resource settings: requests are what the scheduler reserves, limits are enforced ceilings. Exceeding a CPU limit throttles; exceeding a memory limit triggers an OOM kill.
A controller (`autoscaling/v2`) that adjusts a workload's replica count to keep a metric, such as average CPU utilization relative to requests, near a target.
The default Deployment strategy: a new ReplicaSet scales up while the old one scales down, paced by `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` and gated by readiness.
A package of templated Kubernetes manifests plus default values. `helm upgrade --install` deploys it as a numbered release revision that `helm rollback` can return to.
The Kubernetes successor to Ingress for routing external traffic, split into GatewayClass, Gateway and HTTPRoute resources so platform and app teams each own their part.
